blocks.x: We're in a brave new world of PC gaming hardware right now, with extra emphasis on the irony in that phrase. I wrote recently about how there isn't a single well-priced PC left, and that's true if we're comparing prices even to just last year. But the thing is, some people will still want or need to buy a new PC even in this inflated market, and judging by how you folks have responded to our recent polls, many of you are still reluctantly willing to pay the premium for a gaming PC upgrade.

To that end, I shall solider on and deliver the best gaming PC deals I can find to your doorsteps, even if they're expensive compared to last year's market. And right now, just as I reported a few weeks ago, RTX 5070 gaming PCs look to be where it's at for value below $2,000.
Take a look at the other discounted PCs we've spotted or follow us on WhatsApp.

None of the previous RTX 5070 PCs I highlighted are available at those prices anymore, but I've found a couple more, and in fact one of them is even cheaper at $1,399 at B&H Photo—though you have to be willing to compromise on the CPU. Or, if you'd rather compromise on the RAM than the CPU, there's another option for you, for $1,600 at Amazon.
MSI Codex Z2C | Ryzen 7 8700F | $1,399 @ B&H Photo

Codex Z2C | RTX 5070: was $1599 now $1399
The headline here is obviously that you're getting an RTX 5070 in a very reasonably priced rig given the 2026 market. The caveat is that CPU is not a full-fledged desktop one, rather a repurposed power-limited and low-cache chip. It's socket AM5, though, so swapping to a decent Ryzen chip should work wonders.
Key specs: Ryzen 7 8700F | RTX 5070 | 16 GB DDR5 | 1 TB SSDView Deal

Considering 2026 prices, this is the build I would be going for. The thing to highlight from the very start is that CPU is not fantastic. It's actually a repurposed mobile chip, which means it has a low maximum TDP and has just 16 MB of L3 cache. That nerfs it pretty significantly for many uses, however the PC should still be fine for gaming, especially in more GPU-bound games.

What makes the CPU caveat not such a big deal is that it's socket AM5, meaning you can replace it with a decent Ryzen chip and perhaps even an X3D one. Importantly, CPUs are one one kind of component that hasn't seen such a dramatic price increase over the past few months, despite declining sales and yes, murmurs of slight price increases.
And apart from the CPU, you're getting a complete, ready-to-go system with a graphics card that's very capable of 1440p gaming, and some DDR5 RAM to boot.

Gaming Blaze 5 | RTX 5070: was $1699.99 now $1599.99
We're in the time of compromises, it seems, because this might offer some serious gaming grunt for the cost, but it also skims pretty significantly on memory. 16 GB of DDR4-3200 isn't great all-round, but purely for gaming it should be fine. And you're getting a very nice midrange CPU-GPU combo.
Key specs: Core i7 14700F | RTX 5070 | 16 GB DDR4-3200 | 1 TB SSDView Deal

This option is less appealing to my eyes, but if you're certain you won't want to upgrade any of your new PC's components any time soon, it might be a better choice than the MSI one. That's because the CPU here is much more capable than the 8700F in the MSI.

The caveat in this case is you're getting DDR4 RAM rather than DDR5, which means if you do decide you want to upgrade this memory in the future, you'll have to swap your motherboard and CPU out to boot. In other words, you're locking yourself in a bit, here.

You're also paying $200 extra for the privilege, putting it in the range of what I've seen some RX 9070 XT gaming PCs going for recently, which will perform much better and be worth it if you can catch one on sale. So, I'd say this Skytech build is primarily for if you can't stretch your budget much higher and you're sure you won't want to touch it for upgrades any time soon. If that describes you, you'll do fine with this build and will net some great 1440p performance out of most modern games.
